title: Assessment of Acoustic Metawindow unit through psychoacoustic analysis and human perception
research_question: To assess the impact of an Acoustic Metawindow (AMW) unit on environmental indoor human perception through psychoacoustic analysis and human perception evaluation.

participants.description: 40 females, 43 males, 1 non-binary individual, aged 20-60 years old. Nationalities: Europe and North Africa (77%), Asia (19%), America (4%), and Australia (1%).
participants.recruitment: Recruited through the University of Sheffield, A*STAR, University of Perugia students and staff, and residents of Sheffield, Singapore, and Perugia.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Seven environmental sound recordings (#1 Beach, #2 Woodlands, #3 Quiet Street, #4 Pedestrian Zone, #5 Park, #6 Shopping Mall, and #7 Busy Street) presented in two configurations: with and without the Acoustic Metawindow (AMW) unit effect. Total of 14 recordings.

measures.instrument: Aihua AWA6228 sound level meter with built-in FFT analyser
5-point Likert scale (Not at all Loud to Extremely Loud)
5-point Likert scale for eventful, vibrant, pleasant, calm, uneventful, monotonous, annoying, chaotic (ISO TS 12913-2 attribute scales)
5-point Likert scale (Very good to Very bad)

mechanisms: The AMW unit's medium-high frequency filtering capacity (100-4500 Hz) reduces peaks in sound signals, leading to a decrease in psychoacoustic parameters like Loudness, Roughness, and Sharpness.

The AMW unit neutralises high-pitch sound sources, including 'talking' ones (e.g., human voices, car horns, kids playing), which can lead to a perception of increased annoyance and decreased pleasantness when human voices are present, as the brain struggles to elaborate the message.
The AMW unit's effect of reducing vibrancy, chaos, and eventfulness, and increasing monotonousness and uneventfulness, contributes to a general neutralisation of the perceived soundscape.
moderators: Positive interpretation of characterising sound sources (e.g., children playing, people having fun) can moderate the perceived Loudness impact of the AMW unit.
implementation_implications: The AMW unit, due to its neutralising effect on middle/high frequencies, could be suitable for indoor functions requiring a quiet and calm environment, such as libraries, studying rooms, religious places, and meditation rooms.

The customisable acoustic nature of the AMW unit suggests further studies could investigate shifting its neutralising effect to specifically targeted frequency ranges, allowing for tailored designs for different indoor functions and outdoor noise sources.

Designing AMMs-based building features like windows should consider both quantitative (psychoacoustic parameters) and qualitative (human perception/soundscape descriptors) methods for a comprehensive ergonomic and soundscape assessment.

tables.description: RMS of Effectiveness of the AMW unit (EffX) according to four psychoacoustic parameters: Loudness (N), Roughness (R), Sharpness (S), and Fluctuation Strength (FS). Data gathered from three measuring points a, b, c in Figure 2.b. Values are RMS of the values related to the seven considered environmental sound recordings (with and without the AMW unit effect). JND multiples are highlighted in italic, while the highest JND multiple is highlighted in bold format.

limitations: The AMW model used for these experiments was the basic one (without broadband optimisation) due to the current pandemic situation, limiting its noise-reducing capacity over a lower frequency range (50-300Hz) and showing signal magnification at 280Hz.
Further study is needed to clarify if Roughness and Sharpness decrease has a positive or negative impact, depending on the outdoor sound sources.

The study highlights a disagreement between analytical and perceived responses for some recordings (e.g., #5 Park), suggesting that human perception can be influenced by the positive interpretation of sound sources, which is not captured by psychoacoustic parameters alone.
